title: Fewer than 800 Scots have received weight loss jabs on NHS, BBC finds
content:
Fewer than 800 Scots have received jabs for weight loss on the NHS despite them being approved for use three years ago, BBC News has found.
While private prescriptions for Wegovey and Mounjaro have soared, fewer than half of Scotland's health boards currently offer the treatment specifically for weight loss - and then only as part of small pilot schemes.
Leading doctors have described the situation as "discriminatory" and argued that the lack of access on the NHS is widening health inequalities.
The Scottish government said the medicines were part of a range of treatments for obesity, and that individual health boards were responsible for decisions on the availability of medicines.
A third of Scots are classified as obese, which can lead to serious health complications including cardiovascular disease, cancer and diabetes.
Medications like Mounjaro and Wegovy have been prescribed for people with type 2 diabetes for many years, and are thought to have been used by thousands of patients.
These GLP-1 injections suppress people's appetites, causing them to feel fuller sooner - but are not suitable for everyone and can have side effects.
Mounjaro has been approved for use specifically for weight loss on the NHS in Scotland since 2023, and Wegovy was approved in 2024.
We sent a freedom of information request to every health board in Scotland, asking them if they prescribe the jabs to patients specifically for weight loss.
Five told us that they do prescribe the drugs as part of pilot projects which allow a small number of patients to access the jabs on the NHS.
They are: NHS Forth Valley, NHS Borders, NHS Lothian, NHS Lanarkshire, NHS Western Isles and the NHS State Hospital.
The figures showed that a total of 705 patients had received injections for weight loss by September 2026.
It has been estimated that at least 300,000 people are accessing the drugs privately, according to the company Simple Online Pharmacy.
Scotland's nine other health boards say they do not currently routinely prescribe for weight loss specifically, although some are looking to introduce access.
There may be some exceptional circumstances where patients in those areas are able to access the drugs.
Kathleen McClaughlin, from Laurieston, is one of the patients who can access the injections on the NHS.
The 54-year-old was referred to NHS Forth Valley's programme by her gynaecologist because she needs surgery, but her weight was too high for it to go ahead safely.
Having "tried and failed many times" to lose weight, she now has arthritis and other mobility issues.
"It stops your life progressing. You're just vegetating your life away," she said.
Kathleen did not want to pay privately for the jabs, concerned about not having the right support.

title: Kenya confirms second Ebola case - a relative of the first victim
content:
Kenya has confirmed a second case of Ebola, 10 days after a businessman died of the virus after he had travelled to the East African nation from the Democratic Republic of Congo.
The new patient, a 39-year-old man, is a close relative of the first case and was already in quarantine when he fell ill on Tuesday, Kenya's health ministry says.
The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.
Detecting his illness early had improved his chances of recovery and limited the chance of him passing the virus on to others, the ministry said, as it urged the public to "stay calm but vigilant".
"Both cases are linked, and there is no evidence of spread in the wider community," the ministry said.
"Kenya remains open, with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings", it added.
The 40-year-old Kenyan man who died on 5 October was diagnosed with Ebola shortly after being admitted to hospital in the capital, Nairobi.
A relative had taken him there shortly after picking him up at the airport. He had travelled from DR Congo, through Uganda to Kenya without his illness being detected.
Since his death, officials had determined that he had been in contact with 128 people - and since Tuesday 113 of them had been found, the health ministry said.
Of these, 108 were in quarantine in Kenya and tracing of the remaining 15 continued, it said.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.
The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
"Anyone with fever, unusual tiredness, muscle or joint pains, vomiting, diarrhoea or unexplained bleeding should seek care promptly at the nearest health facility," Kenya's health ministry said.
The current outbreak in DR Congo, which began in May, has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died.
However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that county free of the disease in August.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, the continent's leading public health agency, has reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements for the six weeks leading up to his death.
It revealed that he first started feeling unwell in DR Congo on 15 September - and showed how several opportunities to detect the infection were missed, including during several visits to Congolese medical facilities.
He then managed to travel through Uganda to Kenya - and was again not detected at airports screenings.
Health experts say it highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.

title: ‘Boy kibble’: Healthy and convenient or a bowl full of nothing?
content: Ever fill your dog’s dish, look down at the kibble, and feel a little envious? No? Well, for some people the idea of one bowl full of all your nutrients that takes very little thought and effort is an appealing idea — and they are already eating it for many of their meals. It is called “boy kibble,” a way of eating that has made the rounds on social media and basically strips meals back to their basics to deliver high protein as conveniently as possible. “I just look at it as a bowl. What I make it with is ground beef, avocado and rice. That’s it. Super simple,” said content creator and boy kibble connoisseur Nick Finke. Sure, it’s easy, and there can be debate about whether it is appetizing for all people, but is it a healthy dietary plan? Boy kibble is the other side of another trend –– “girl dinner.” Both emphasize convenience and reduce thought, but where girl dinner grabs various snacks already available to cobble together a meal (think some cheese, crackers, cherry tomatoes and a yogurt), boy kibble is batch cooking and eating the same thing every night. Usually that means a rice base with ground meat –– turkey, chicken or beef. Some people add a variety of spices or seasonings, but some don’t. Finke also adds avocado to get healthy fat in the meal as well. This isn’t an occasional menu item or a convenient back up plan if he doesn’t want to cook. Finke said he eats boy kibble every night. “It’s super easy to meal prep,” Finke said. “I just batch my ground beef at the beginning of the week and my rice, and then I have it for lunch or dinner every single day of the week.” Boy kibble can be for anyone, Finke said, but it has been particular popular with men. And men who are looking to increase their fitness really resonate with this simplified way of eating. One of the biggest benefits of eating this is way, according to those who adopt it, is a reliable way to meet protein goals. Those can be high for people trying to put on muscle, said Dr. Zachary Mulvihill, integrative medicine expert at Weill Cornell Medicine and NewYork-Presbyterian. And protein is an important nutrient, but recently people have been taking it to the extreme, said Natalie Mokari, a dietitian based in Charlotte, North Carolina. One problem with boy kibble is that the ratios are off from what experts typically recommend. Generally, people should aim for half of their plate to be vegetables, one quarter to be carbohydrates and one quarter protein, Mulvihill said. But this plan is half protein and half carbohydrates with vegetables often optional. Finke said that while he eats boy kibble for most dinners, he focuses on vegetables in other meals. The Mediterranean diet has been hailed as one of the healthiest styles of eating for longevity and lower disease risk , and boy kibble does stray from the method in its heavy reliance on animal proteins and low diversity of plants, Mulvihill said. Experts like this trend but aren’t subscribing outright. Boy kibble might be helpful … with some caveats, both Mokari and Mulvihill said. It’s good to move more toward home-prepared, whole ingredient meals instead of relying on restaurants or pre-prepared meals, and it’s great if boy kibble helps you do that, Mulvihill said. However, Mokari does recommend making some additions for a more balanced diet. Adding in some vegetables, even if they are precut or frozen to increase convenience, is a great way to round the meal out, she said. Long term, eating the same meal every day limits the variety of nutrients a person gets, so Mulvihill recommends that people who benefit from a repetitive diet to eat more whole, homecooked meals build in times where they switch it up. “This can be a good starting point for some people,” Mokari said.
